The pigmentation intensity was most pronounced on the face, neck, and upper torso (Fig. 1).

report.source_text: Four months later, a diagnostic skin biopsy was taken from his right shoulder area and revealed intracellular and extracellular melanin deposition in the dermis. Intracellular deposition of melanin was detected in two types of cells: CD68(+) macrophages and melanoma metastatic cells with immunohistochemical profile: Melan-A (+), HMB45 (+), S100(+), CD68 (−), distributed and grouped into deep layers of the dermis (Fig. 3).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 72-year-old man with a history of high-risk melanoma (2011: nodular type, Clark IV, Breslow >3 mm, with sentinel node subcapsular metastasis) presented to the Dermatology Department with a 4-month history of dark gray skin pigmentation predominantly affecting the face, neck, and upper torso. He reported concurrent systemic symptoms including general weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss, and dark urine. Prior hospitalization in the Internal Diseases Department 2 weeks before Dermatology admission excluded Addison's disease and porphyria as alternative diagnoses. Diagnostic skin biopsy from the right shoulder revealed intracellular and extracellular melanin deposition in the dermis, with melanoma metastatic cells identified by immunohistochemistry (Melan-A+, HMB45+, S100+, CD68−). Comprehensive imaging (ultrasonography, chest X-ray, CT, colonoscopy, PET-CT) identified a 2 cm tumor in the right kidney. Urinalysis showed brown-amber discoloration without other abnormalities. The patient refused treatment and died 8 months after the onset of DMC. The diagnosis of diffuse melanin cutis secondary to metastatic melanoma was established based on the pathological confirmation of melanoma metastatic cells in the dermis producing melanin deposition, in the clinical context of a high-risk melanoma history and systemic metastatic disease.
